summary: Provides a framework and practical guidance for deploying In situ Operations, Administration, and Maintenance, which records operational and telemetry data inside packets as they cross a path. It covers deployment considerations. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Packets pick up little notes about each stop on their trip, and this guide explains how to set that up in a real network.

questions: how to deploy in situ oam
subtitle: Framework and guidance for deploying in-band network telemetry to monitor packet journeys.

tldr.problem: Network operators need detailed visibility into how packets traverse their networks—their paths, delays, queue depths, and other per-hop details. Traditional active probing (ping, traceroute) does not capture data on actual traffic.
tldr.mechanism: IOAM collects telemetry data inside regular user packets as they traverse a network domain. Each hop along the path records information such as node identity, interface IDs, timestamps, and queue occupancy directly in the packet header.
tldr.outcome: Operators gain real-time visibility into packet paths, per-hop delays, and network behavior for live traffic without sending extra probe packets. IOAM supports multiple operational modes including per-hop tracing, proof of transit verification, and edge-to-edge measurement.

facts.label: Target scope
facts.value: Limited network domains, not the global Internet

today: RFC 9378 is an Informational RFC published in April 2023, complementing RFC 9197 which defines the IOAM data formats. Together they form the authoritative guidance for deploying IOAM in production networks. IOAM is in active development and adoption in data centers and service provider networks.

sections.title: What Is IOAM and Why Deploy It
sections.content:
In situ Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (IOAM) is a mechanism for collecting operational telemetry data inside data packets as they traverse a network. The term "in situ" means the data is embedded directly in the packets traveling through the network, rather than sent in separate probe packets. IOAM complements active measurement tools like ping and traceroute, but captures data from actual user traffic.

IOAM is useful for proving that traffic follows expected paths (such as through a service function chain), verifying Service Level Agreements (SLAs) on live traffic, understanding how multipath networks distribute traffic across parallel paths, and detecting when probe traffic is treated differently from regular data traffic. Unlike simple ping or traceroute, IOAM provides detailed per-hop metrics on real packets.
sections.plainLanguage: IOAM lets you attach notes to packets as they travel, so you see exactly what happens at each hop. It's like putting a journal in a letter instead of sending a separate report.

sections.title: IOAM Domains and Node Roles
sections.content:
IOAM is designed for use within limited, bounded network domains, not the global Internet. An IOAM-Domain is a single network under one operator's control—such as a campus, a data center, or a service provider's internal network. Operators must ensure that packets carrying IOAM data do not leak beyond the domain's edge, using packet filtering if necessary. Network links within the domain must have sufficient MTU to accommodate the extra data IOAM adds to packets.

Each domain contains three types of nodes: IOAM encapsulating nodes add IOAM headers to selected packets, IOAM transit nodes update and add per-hop data as packets pass through, and IOAM decapsulating nodes remove IOAM headers at the domain edge and may export the collected data. A single node can play different roles for different IOAM-Namespaces, allowing flexible deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: An IOAM-Domain is a network under one owner. Entry nodes attach the telemetry, middle nodes add notes, and exit nodes remove it.

sections.title: Four Modes of IOAM Operation
sections.content:
IOAM supports four distinct operational modes. Per-Hop Tracing collects data at each node the packet traverses, capturing node ID, ingress and egress interface IDs, timestamps, queue depths, and generic operator-defined data. This mode reveals the full path taken by packets and per-hop delays. Proof of Transit (POT) verifies that a packet has traversed a specific expected path or service chain, using nested hashing or encryption to prove which nodes were visited.

Edge-to-Edge (E2E) collects data only at the entry and exit of the IOAM-Domain, measuring overall delay, jitter, and domain-level telemetry without per-hop overhead. Direct Export sends per-hop data directly to a collector instead of carrying it in the packet, useful when per-hop tracing would make packets too large. Each mode serves different operational needs and scaling constraints.
sections.plainLanguage: Trace mode: see every hop. POT mode: prove you went the right way. E2E mode: only measure entry and exit. Export mode: send data to a collector instead of in the packet.

sections.title: Transporting IOAM and Exporting Data
sections.content:
IOAM data can be encapsulated in multiple transport protocols: IPv6 Hop-by-Hop extension headers, NSH (Network Service Header), BIER (Bit Index Explicit Replication), GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation), Geneve, Segment Routing, and VXLAN-GPE. The choice of encapsulation depends on the network architecture and the protocol already in use.

IOAM data is extracted at the decapsulating node and exported using industry-standard mechanisms such as IPFIX (IP Flow Information Export). The RFC introduces a key architectural pattern: separation of concerns. IOAM data-plane operations (adding and updating data) are handled by forwarding engines on network nodes, while interpretation and aggregation of IOAM data are handled by separate data-processing systems. This decoupling allows high-performance routers to forward packets without the overhead of analyzing the telemetry data they collect.
sections.plainLanguage: IOAM data can ride inside various packet types. When it reaches the end, it gets exported to a system that makes sense of it.

sections.title: Practical Considerations for Deployment
sections.content:
Deployments must address IOAM-Namespaces, which provide context and isolation for IOAM-Data-Fields. Different namespaces allow operators to deploy IOAM on different device types, use different timestamp formats, and separate operational domains, even within the same network. IOAM Layering allows IOAM at multiple protocol levels (for example, at both IPv6 and Geneve layers in a tunneled deployment), with each layer operating independently.

The RFC discusses two trace option types: Pre-allocated Trace, where the encapsulating node allocates space for all hops upfront (efficient for software forwarders), and Incremental Trace, where each node appends its data (better for hardware forwarders). Operators can also limit which traffic IOAM applies to using per-interface or access-control-list rules, enable Loopback to measure the return path as well, and Active Flag to mark synthetic probe packets. For gradual rollouts, brown-field deployments can mix IOAM-aware and IOAM-unaware nodes; IOAM-unaware nodes simply forward packets unchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: Choose whether to record all hops upfront or let each node add its data. Pick a namespace to isolate your deployment. Decide which traffic gets telemetry. Some devices might not support IOAM; that's okay, they just pass packets through.

sections.title: Management and Security
sections.content:
IOAM deployment is configured and managed using YANG models, enabling integration with standard network management systems. The RFC points to IOAM profiles, which define constrained subsets of the full IOAM specification for specific use cases, reducing implementation complexity and improving interoperability testing. Capability discovery tools can help identify which IOAM features each node in the domain supports.

Like all OAM mechanisms, IOAM must be protected from attack. Operators must control which traffic enters the IOAM-Domain and prevent packets with IOAM headers from leaking out. Because IOAM data can reveal network structure and performance, access to exported IOAM data should be restricted. The separation of data-plane and control-plane roles helps contain the blast radius of any security issue.
sections.plainLanguage: Use standard configuration tools to manage IOAM. Keep IOAM data contained within your network. Restrict who can see the exported telemetry.

items.text: Verify that a packet traversed an expected path or service chain.
